title: Grammar: articles & markers
description: How these languages mark nouns and structure sentences.

steps.title: Nouns and their markers
steps.body: Haitian Creole, Korean, and Chinese each handle definiteness and nouns very differently from European languages.

steps.title: Key differences
steps.body: No language in this group has gender like French or Spanish.
bullets: Haitian Creole: definite article la/a/an comes AFTER the noun; no gender
Korean: no articles; topic (은/는) and subject (이/가) markers do important grammar work
Chinese: no articles, no gender; measure words are required between numbers and nouns

steps.explanation: In Haitian Creole, the definite article la/a/an comes AFTER the noun: tab la = the table. There is no gender.

steps.title: Check
steps.prompt: Where does the definite article go in Haitian Creole?
options: At the end of the sentence
steps.explanation: In Haitian Creole, the definite article (la/a/an) always follows the noun: tab la, kay a.

steps.title: Check · plural
steps.prompt: How do you make a noun plural and definite in Haitian Creole?
steps.explanation: Yo marks plural definiteness: timoun yo = the children.

steps.title: Check · gender
steps.prompt: Which statement about Haitian Creole gender is correct?
options: Has masculine and feminine gender like French
Has gender that changes adjective forms
steps.explanation: Haitian Creole has no grammatical gender. Tab and kay are just nouns with no gender.

description: The core verbs — and how they differ across languages.

steps.title: Workhorses
steps.body: The concepts of "to be" and "to have" exist in all three languages but work quite differently.

steps.title: Listen · identity
steps.prompt: How do you say "She is Haitian"?
Say you're tired and hungry:
options: Mwen grangou e mwen fatige se.
Fatige mwen ye e grangou mwen gen.
steps.explanation: Both tiredness and hunger use the same structure with mwen + adjective in Haitian Creole.

steps.title: Check · se
steps.prompt: How do you say "I am Haitian" (identity)?
steps.explanation: Se is used for identity: Mwen se Ayisyen = I am Haitian.

steps.title: Check · gen
steps.prompt: "Mwen gen yon rezèvasyon" means…
steps.explanation: Gen = to have; Mwen gen yon rezèvasyon = I have a reservation.

steps.title: Check · adjective
steps.prompt: How do you say "they are hungry" in Haitian Creole?
steps.explanation: In Haitian Creole, adjectives follow the subject directly: Yo grangou (they hungry = they are hungry).

title: Verbs & patterns
description: How verbs work in these three languages.

steps.title: Verb patterns
steps.body: Haitian Creole verbs don't conjugate at all — the biggest advantage for learners! Korean and Chinese also avoid the complexity of European conjugation.

steps.title: Verb patterns compared
steps.body: These languages express tense and aspect very differently.
bullets: Haitian Creole: verbs never change. Aspect markers (ap, te, pral) are added.
Korean: verbs conjugate for politeness and tense, but not for person or gender.
Chinese: verbs never change. Tense is shown by time words and aspect particles (了, 过, 着).

steps.prompt: Match each Haitian Creole word with its English meaning:
Arrange the stones to say: "I speak a little Creole.":
steps.explanation: The verb pattern in action — master this form and unlock a whole verb family.

steps.title: Listen · aspect
steps.prompt: Which form means "I am speaking right now" (progressive)?
Say yes, you speak a little Creole:
options: Wi, mwen pale yon ti kreyòl.
Wi, ou pale yon ti kreyòl.
Wi, nou pale yon ti kreyòl.
steps.correctAnswer: Wi, mwen pale yon ti kreyòl.
steps.explanation: In Haitian Creole, verbs don't conjugate — mwen pale means "I speak". Pronouns show the subject.

steps.title: Check · no conjugation
steps.prompt: In Haitian Creole, do verbs change based on the subject (I, you, he…)?
steps.explanation: Haitian Creole verbs never conjugate. Mwen pale = I speak; Li pale = She speaks. Same verb form.

steps.title: Check · aspect
steps.prompt: What does "ap" signal before a verb in Haitian Creole?
steps.explanation: Ap marks the present progressive: mwen ap manje = I am eating right now.

title: Adjectives & descriptions
description: How descriptive words work in these languages.

steps.title: Describing things
steps.body: None of these three languages has the gender agreement of European Romance languages, which simplifies adjective use significantly.

steps.title: Key rules
steps.body: Adjectives work simply in these languages.
bullets: Haitian Creole: adjectives never change for gender or number
Korean: adjectives conjugate like verbs (for tense/politeness) but not for gender/number of the noun
Chinese: adjectives don't change form; predicative adjectives usually take 很 (hěn)

steps.prompt: Match each Haitian Creole word with its English meaning:
Arrange the stones to say: "She is small.":
steps.explanation: Agreement at work: the adjective shifts to match the noun it describes.

steps.title: Listen · adjective
steps.prompt: Which adjective form goes with "sè" (sister)?

steps.partnerSays: Frè mwen wo. E sè ou?
steps.partnerSaysTranslation: My brother is tall. And your sister?
steps.prompt: Describe your sister the same way:
steps.explanation: In Haitian Creole, adjectives do NOT change for gender or number: wo works for everyone.

steps.title: Check · no agreement
steps.prompt: In Haitian Creole, how does "tall" (wo) change for a woman?
steps.explanation: Haitian Creole adjectives never change for gender or number: wo works for everyone.

steps.title: Check · position
steps.prompt: Where do adjectives usually go in Haitian Creole?
steps.explanation: Haitian Creole adjectives typically follow the noun: yon gason wo (a tall man), but can precede: bèl bagay (beautiful thing).

title: Saying no
description: Turn any sentence negative with simple patterns.

steps.title: Negation patterns
steps.body: Each language has a characteristic way to negate a verb. Learn the pattern, apply it everywhere.

steps.title: Patterns compared
steps.body: Negation is relatively straightforward in all three languages.
bullets: Haitian Creole: pa before the verb
Korean: 안 before verb/adjective, or -지 않다 after the stem
Chinese: 不 (bù) for general negation, 没 (méi) for past/existence

steps.prompt: Match each Haitian Creole word with its English meaning:
Arrange the stones to say: "I don't like coffee.":
steps.explanation: The negation pattern in its simplest form — learn it once, use it everywhere.

steps.title: Listen · pa
steps.prompt: Which is the correct negative form?
Say no, you don't like coffee:
steps.explanation: Haitian Creole negation: pa goes directly after the subject pronoun and before the verb.

steps.title: Check · placement
steps.prompt: Where does "pa" go in a Haitian Creole negative sentence?
steps.explanation: Pa goes directly before the verb: mwen pa pale, mwen pa renmen.

steps.title: Check · never
steps.prompt: How do you say "I never eat" in Haitian Creole?
steps.explanation: Pa janm = never: mwen pa janm manje = I never eat.

title: Asking questions
description: Question words and patterns.

steps.title: Asking around
steps.body: Each language has its own set of question words and question-formation patterns.

steps.title: Patterns compared
steps.body: Yes/no and information questions each have their own structure.
bullets: Haitian Creole: eske at the start for yes/no; question word replaces the unknown element
Korean: question words in place of what they ask; -요? at the end for polite questions
Chinese: question words in place of what they ask; 吗 (ma) at the end for yes/no questions

steps.prompt: Match each Haitian Creole word with its English meaning:

steps.explanation: A well-formed question using the key structure — polite, clear, and natural.

steps.title: Listen · why
steps.prompt: How do you say "why" in Haitian Creole?
Ask where she lives:
steps.explanation: Question word + subject + verb is the standard order in Haitian Creole questions.

steps.title: Check · word meaning
steps.prompt: How do you say "why" in Haitian Creole?
steps.explanation: Poukisa = why; it pairs with paske (because) in the answer.

steps.title: Check · yes/no question
steps.prompt: Which word forms yes/no questions in Haitian Creole?
steps.explanation: Eske at the start of a statement turns it into a yes/no question.
